passages.quote:
These materials can help industry bodies, membership organisations and other partners introduce self-employed creatives to government guidance on intellectual property (IP).

The guidance on protecting your creative work has been co-created with creative industry partners for self-employed creators. Highlighting the importance of understanding copyright and other intellectual property rights to protect their creative work, retain control over how it is used, and make informed decisions about their rights.

This page includes suggested social media posts, case study posts, newsletter and email copy, checklist templates, presentation slides and digital assets to help you promote the guidance through your channels.

How to use this content

Use the suggested copy and assets in your social media, newsletters, emails, websites and events

Adapt examples, terminology and imagery to suit your sector and audience, while retaining the core messages

Use the checklist templates to introduce practical questions relevant to your audience, rather than as a substitute for the guidance

Signpost a quick guide to protecting your creative work so your audience can read the guidance and find further support.

Use the presentation pack in webinars, workshops and other industry events.

The materials are intended to raise awareness and signpost the guidance. They do not provide legal advice.

Social media posts

Launch social media announcement – generic post

New government guidance is available to help self-employed creatives understand how to manage their intellectual property when creating, collaborating, sharing or selling their work. Read the guidance on self-employed creatives and check what you should consider before starting your next project.

Collaboration social media posts

Working with others on a project, production and commission? Before you start, discuss who owns each contribution, how the finished work can be used and whether anyone can reuse it later. Record what you agree in writing. Explore the government guidance on self-employed creatives.

Licensing social media post

Someone wants to use your image, writing, music and designs? Before agreeing, be clear about what they can use, where they can use it and for how long. Check that the written terms reflect your understanding. Explore the government on self-employed creatives.

Case study social media posts

Paule Constable – lighting designer

Notes - not for publication

Role of the case study - help creatives recognise that questions about their contribution can extend beyond finished production to the files, records and future use of work.

Audience-facing copy: short-form post

A production ends - but what happens when the work is revived?

Lighting designer Paule Constable describes disputes over access to files recording designs and the reuse of creative work.

Working with others? Explore questions about ownership, access and future use.

Audience-facing copy: longer-form post

Title: The performance has finished. The questions about your work may not have.

Lighting designer Paule Constable works across theatre, opera, dance and musical theatre. Her account describes uncertainty over access to files documenting lighting designs, as well as disputes about designs being reused in other productions.

In one example, a third party attempted to charge a producer to release data relating to her designs. She also describes the difficulty of challenging productions that copied elements of original designs.

For self-employed creatives, these experiences raise practical questions: who owns each contribution, who can access the files needed to use it, and what has been agreed about future productions or reuse?

If you collaborate on performances or other creative projects, explore the government guidance to understand the ownership and contracting questions you may need to consider.
